concept.title: Knots That Think: Cognition as Braiding in Category Theory
concept.concept_description: The brain's connectome is a braid: neurons fire in sequences that interleave like strands of a braid group. Formalize this: a cognitive process is an element of the braid group B_n where n is the number of brain regions. Two cognitive processes are equivalent if their braids are related by Reidemeister moves (cognitive equivalence). Conjecture: The Jones polynomial of a cognitive braid is invariant under cognitive equivalence and encodes the information content of the thought. A thought with Jones polynomial V(t) = 1 is a trivial thought (equivalent to no thinking). A thought with V(t) = -t^2 + t + 1 is a creative thought (it contains a trefoil knot — the simplest non-trivial braid). The information content of a thought is log(|V(e^{2pi i/3})|), which measures the quantum dimension of the braid. Test: compute the Jones polynomial of braids representing simple cognitive processes (linear reasoning: trivial braid, creative insight: trefoil, confused thinking: figure-eight knot) and verify that the quantum dimension correlates with subjective ratings of thought quality. Impact: thinking IS braiding. The topology of your thoughts determines their quality. Creative insights are literally knotted.

# Semicubes in hypercubes and their Helly properties

A vertex of the hypercube `Q(ι)` is identified with a finite subset `s : Finset ι`
(its "support", i.e. the set of coordinates equal to `1`).  Given a coordinate
`i : ι` and a bit `b : Bool`, the *semicube* `semicube ι i b` is the set of all
vertices whose `i`-th coordinate (membership of `i`) equals `b`.

This file develops, in strict layers:

* **Layer 1** – basic combinatorics of semicubes (`semicube_complement`,
  `semicube_inter_opposite`);
* **Layer 2** – a Helly-type theorem for a finite family of semicubes proved
  *from first principles* (`semicube_helly2`), using no Helly theorem;
* **Layer 3** – the behaviour of semicubes under Cartesian products of
  subgraphs of hypercubes (`product_semicube_decomposition`) and the reduction
  of the opposite-semicube Helly property to the two factors
  (`product_helly_reduction`).

All results, including the final product theorem, are proved with complete
proofs (no `sorry`).
-/

open Finset

namespace SemicubeHelly

/-! ## Layer 1: basic semicube properties -/

/-- The semicube of the hypercube `Q(ι)` at coordinate `i` with bit `b`:
the finite set of all vertices `s : Finset ι` whose `i`-th coordinate equals `b`. -/
def semicube (ι : Type*) [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] (i : ι) (b : Bool) :
    Finset (Finset ι) :=
  Finset.univ.filter (fun s => decide (i ∈ s) = b)

variable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]

@[simp] lemma mem_semicube {i : ι} {b : Bool} {s : Finset ι} :
    s ∈ semicube ι i b ↔ decide (i ∈ s) = b := by
  simp [semicube]

/--
`semicube i true` and `semicube i false` are disjoint and cover the whole
vertex set.
-/
theorem semicube_complement (i : ι) :
    Disjoint (semicube ι i true) (semicube ι i false) ∧
      semicube ι i true ∪ semicube ι i false = Finset.univ := by
  exact ⟨ Finset.disjoint_filter.mpr fun _ _ _ _ => by aesop, Finset.eq_univ_of_forall fun s => by by_cases hi : i ∈ s <;> aesop ⟩

/--
Two semicubes `semicube i b` and `semicube j c` intersect iff either the
coordinates differ (`i ≠ j`) or the bits agree (`b = c`).
-/
theorem semicube_inter_opposite (i j : ι) (b c : Bool) :
    (semicube ι i b ∩ semicube ι j c).Nonempty ↔ (i ≠ j ∨ b = c) := by
  by_cases h : i = j <;> simp_all +decide [ SemicubeHelly.semicube ];
  · cases b <;> cases c <;> simp +decide [ Finset.Nonempty ];
    · exact ⟨ ∅, by simp +decide ⟩;
    · exact ⟨ { j }, Finset.mem_singleton_self _ ⟩;
  · refine' ⟨ if b then { i } ∪ if c then { j } else ∅ else if c then { j } else ∅, _ ⟩ ; aesop ( simp_config := { decide := true } ) ;

/-! ## Layer 2: Helly property from first principles -/

/-- A finite family of semicubes, encoded as a finite set of `(coordinate, bit)`
pairs, has the *pairwise intersection property* if every two of its members
intersect. -/
def SemicubePairwise (F : Finset (ι × Bool)) : Prop :=
  ∀ p ∈ F, ∀ q ∈ F, (semicube ι p.1 p.2 ∩ semicube ι q.1 q.2).Nonempty

/--
**Helly property for semicubes.** Any finite family of semicubes with the
pairwise intersection property has a common vertex.  Proved from first
principles, using only `semicube_inter_opposite`.
-/
theorem semicube_helly2 (F : Finset (ι × Bool)) (hF : SemicubePairwise F) :
    ∃ s : Finset ι, ∀ p ∈ F, s ∈ semicube ι p.1 p.2 := by
  by_contra! h_contra;
  -- Let's define the set `T` as the set of all coordinates `i` such that `(i, true) ∈ F`.
  set T := F.filter (fun p => p.2 = true) |>.image Prod.fst with hT_def;
  obtain ⟨ p, hp₁, hp₂ ⟩ := h_contra T;
  cases h : p.2 <;> simp_all +decide [ semicube ];
  · have := hF _ hp₁ _ hp₂; simp_all +decide [ semicube_inter_opposite ] ;
  · grind

/-! ## Layer 3: product reduction -/

/-- Embedding of a pair of vertices (one in each factor) into the vertex set of
the product hypercube `Q(ι₁ ⊕ ι₂)`. -/
def embedPair {ι₁ ι₂ : Type*} [DecidableEq ι₁] [DecidableEq ι₂]
    (p : Finset ι₁ × Finset ι₂) : Finset (ι₁ ⊕ ι₂) :=
  p.1.map ⟨Sum.inl, Sum.inl_injective⟩ ∪ p.2.map ⟨Sum.inr, Sum.inr_injective⟩

/-- Vertex set of the Cartesian product `G₁ □ G₂` of two subgraphs of hypercubes,
embedded into `Q(ι₁ ⊕ ι₂)`. -/
def prodV {ι₁ ι₂ : Type*} [DecidableEq ι₁] [DecidableEq ι₂]
    (V₁ : Finset (Finset ι₁)) (V₂ : Finset (Finset ι₂)) :
    Finset (Finset (ι₁ ⊕ ι₂)) :=
  (V₁ ×ˢ V₂).image embedPair

/-- The semicube of a subgraph with vertex set `V ⊆ Q(κ)` at coordinate `i`,
bit `b`: the vertices of `V` whose `i`-th coordinate equals `b`. -/
def GSemicube {κ : Type*} [DecidableEq κ] (V : Finset (Finset κ)) (i : κ) (b : Bool) :
    Finset (Finset κ) :=
  V.filter (fun v => decide (i ∈ v) = b)

@[simp] lemma mem_GSemicube {κ : Type*} [DecidableEq κ] {V : Finset (Finset κ)}
    {i : κ} {b : Bool} {v : Finset κ} :
    v ∈ GSemicube V i b ↔ v ∈ V ∧ decide (i ∈ v) = b := by
  simp [GSemicube]

/-- The *opposite-semicube Helly property* for a subgraph with vertex set `V`:
any family of semicubes closed under taking opposites and with the pairwise
intersection property has a common vertex. -/
def OppHelly {κ : Type*} [DecidableEq κ] (V : Finset (Finset κ)) : Prop :=
  ∀ F : Finset (κ × Bool), (∀ p ∈ F, (p.1, !p.2) ∈ F) →
    (∀ p ∈ F, ∀ q ∈ F, (GSemicube V p.1 p.2 ∩ GSemicube V q.1 q.2).Nonempty) →
    ∃ v ∈ V, ∀ p ∈ F, v ∈ GSemicube V p.1 p.2

variable {ι₁ ι₂ : Type*} [Fintype ι₁] [DecidableEq ι₁] [Fintype ι₂] [DecidableEq ι₂]

/--
A semicube of the product `G₁ □ G₂` at a left coordinate `Sum.inl i` is the
product of the corresponding left semicube of `G₁` with the whole right factor.
-/
theorem product_semicube_decomposition_left (V₁ : Finset (Finset ι₁))
    (V₂ : Finset (Finset ι₂)) (i : ι₁) (b : Bool) :
    GSemicube (prodV V₁ V₂) (Sum.inl i) b =
      ((GSemicube V₁ i b) ×ˢ V₂).image embedPair := by
  ext v
  simp [GSemicube, prodV, mem_GSemicube, Finset.mem_image, Finset.mem_product, embedPair, Finset.mem_union, Finset.mem_map, Function.Embedding.coeFn_mk];
  grind +suggestions

/--
A semicube of the product `G₁ □ G₂` at a right coordinate `Sum.inr j` is the
product of the whole left factor with the corresponding right semicube of `G₂`.
-/
theorem product_semicube_decomposition_right (V₁ : Finset (Finset ι₁))
    (V₂ : Finset (Finset ι₂)) (j : ι₂) (b : Bool) :
    GSemicube (prodV V₁ V₂) (Sum.inr j) b =
      (V₁ ×ˢ (GSemicube V₂ j b)).image embedPair := by
  simp +decide [ Finset.ext_iff, mem_GSemicube, prodV, embedPair ];
  grind

/-- **Product decomposition of semicubes.** Every semicube in the product
`G₁ □ G₂` decomposes as a left semicube times the right vertex set, or the left
vertex set times a right semicube, according to whether its coordinate lives in
the left or right factor. -/
theorem product_semicube_decomposition (V₁ : Finset (Finset ι₁))
    (V₂ : Finset (Finset ι₂)) (k : ι₁ ⊕ ι₂) (b : Bool) :
    GSemicube (prodV V₁ V₂) k b =
      (Sum.elim
        (fun i => ((GSemicube V₁ i b) ×ˢ V₂).image embedPair)
        (fun j => (V₁ ×ˢ (GSemicube V₂ j b)).image embedPair)) k := by
  cases k with
  | inl i => simpa using product_semicube_decomposition_left V₁ V₂ i b
  | inr j => simpa using product_semicube_decomposition_right V₁ V₂ j b

/-- Membership of a left coordinate in an embedded pair only depends on the left component. -/
lemma inl_mem_embedPair (v₁ : Finset ι₁) (v₂ : Finset ι₂) (i : ι₁) :
    Sum.inl i ∈ embedPair (v₁, v₂) ↔ i ∈ v₁ := by
  simp [embedPair, Finset.mem_union, Finset.mem_map, Function.Embedding.coeFn_mk]

/-- Membership of a right coordinate in an embedded pair only depends on the right component. -/
lemma inr_mem_embedPair (v₁ : Finset ι₁) (v₂ : Finset ι₂) (j : ι₂) :
    Sum.inr j ∈ embedPair (v₁, v₂) ↔ j ∈ v₂ := by
  simp [embedPair, Finset.mem_union, Finset.mem_map, Function.Embedding.coeFn_mk]

/-- An embedded pair of vertices, one from each factor, is a vertex of the product. -/
lemma embedPair_mem_prodV {V₁ : Finset (Finset ι₁)} {V₂ : Finset (Finset ι₂)}
    {v₁ : Finset ι₁} {v₂ : Finset ι₂} (h₁ : v₁ ∈ V₁) (h₂ : v₂ ∈ V₂) :
    embedPair (v₁, v₂) ∈ prodV V₁ V₂ := by
  simp only [prodV, Finset.mem_image]
  exact ⟨(v₁, v₂), by simp [Finset.mem_product, h₁, h₂], rfl⟩

/-- The opposite-semicube Helly property forces the vertex set to be nonempty
(apply it to the empty family). -/
lemma oppHelly_nonempty {κ : Type*} [DecidableEq κ] {V : Finset (Finset κ)}
    (h : OppHelly V) : V.Nonempty := by
  obtain ⟨v, hv, -⟩ := h ∅ (by simp) (by simp)
  exact ⟨v, hv⟩

/--
**Product Helly reduction.** If both factors `G₁` and `G₂` satisfy the
opposite-semicube Helly property, then so does their product `G₁ □ G₂`.

Proof: split the family `F` into the sub-families of left semicubes and right
semicubes.  Each descends to a family on the corresponding factor which is
closed under opposites and pairwise-intersecting (cross pairs, one left one
right, always intersect and impose no constraint on the other factor).  Applying
the factor Helly property yields common vertices `v₁` and `v₂`; their embedded
pair is a common vertex of the product family.
-/
theorem product_helly_reduction (V₁ : Finset (Finset ι₁))
    (V₂ : Finset (Finset ι₂)) (h₁ : OppHelly V₁) (h₂ : OppHelly V₂) :
    OppHelly (prodV V₁ V₂) := by
  intro F hopp hpair
  set F₁ := Finset.filter (fun q => (Sum.inl q.1, q.2) ∈ F) (Finset.univ : Finset (ι₁ × Bool))
  set F₂ := Finset.filter (fun q => (Sum.inr q.1, q.2) ∈ F) (Finset.univ : Finset (ι₂ × Bool));
  -- By the properties of $F₁$ and $F₂$, we know that they are closed under opposites and pairwise intersecting.
  have hF₁_closed : ∀ p ∈ F₁, (p.1, !p.2) ∈ F₁ := by
    grind
  have hF₁_pairwise : ∀ p ∈ F₁, ∀ q ∈ F₁, (GSemicube V₁ p.1 p.2 ∩ GSemicube V₁ q.1 q.2).Nonempty := by
    intro p hp q hq
    specialize hpair (Sum.inl p.1, p.2) (by
    exact Finset.mem_filter.mp hp |>.2) (Sum.inl q.1, q.2) (by
    exact Finset.mem_filter.mp hq |>.2);
    obtain ⟨ w, hw ⟩ := hpair;
    obtain ⟨ w₁, w₂, hw₁, hw₂ ⟩ : ∃ w₁ ∈ GSemicube V₁ p.1 p.2, ∃ w₂ ∈ V₂, w = embedPair (w₁, w₂) := by
      have := product_semicube_decomposition_left V₁ V₂ p.1 p.2;
      grind +splitImp;
    use w₁; simp_all +decide [ embedPair ] ;
  have hF₂_closed : ∀ p ∈ F₂, (p.1, !p.2) ∈ F₂ := by
    grind
  have hF₂_pairwise : ∀ p ∈ F₂, ∀ q ∈ F₂, (GSemicube V₂ p.1 p.2 ∩ GSemicube V₂ q.1 q.2).Nonempty := by
    intro p hp q hq; specialize hpair ( Sum.inr p.1, p.2 ) ( Finset.mem_filter.mp hp |>.2 ) ( Sum.inr q.1, q.2 ) ( Finset.mem_filter.mp hq |>.2 ) ; simp_all +decide [ Finset.Nonempty ] ;
    obtain ⟨ x, hx₁, hx₂, hx₃ ⟩ := hpair; unfold prodV at hx₁ hx₂; simp_all +decide [ Finset.mem_image ] ;
    rcases hx₂ with ⟨ a, b, ⟨ ha, hb ⟩, rfl ⟩ ; use b; simp_all +decide [ embedPair ] ;
  obtain ⟨v₁, hv₁⟩ := h₁ F₁ hF₁_closed hF₁_pairwise
  obtain ⟨v₂, hv₂⟩ := h₂ F₂ hF₂_closed hF₂_pairwise
  use embedPair (v₁, v₂);
  grind +locals

end SemicubeHelly

# Computational Evidence — Semicubes, the Helly property, and Cartesian products

We model the hypercube `Q(ι)` over an index set `ι` by taking a vertex to be a finite
set `A : Finset ι` (the coordinates equal to `1`), with Hamming distance
`hdist A B = |A △ B|`. A **semicube** is a coordinate half-space: for a coordinate `i`
and a sign `b`, `semicube i b` is `{A | i ∈ A}` when `b = true` and `{A | i ∉ A}` when
`b = false`. The **opposite** of `semicube i b` is `semicube i (¬b)`.

## 1. Small-case calculations (pairwise vs. global intersection)

Take `ι = Fin 2`. Consider the family of semicubes indexed by
`s = {(0,true), (1,false)}`.

* `semicube 0 true = {A | 0 ∈ A}`.
* `semicube 1 false = {A | 1 ∉ A}`.
* Pairwise intersection: `{A | 0 ∈ A ∧ 1 ∉ A} = {{0}}` — nonempty.
* Global intersection: same set — nonempty. Witness `A = {0}`.

Now add a conflicting pair `s = {(0,true), (0,false)}`.

* `semicube 0 true ∩ semicube 0 false = {A | 0 ∈ A ∧ 0 ∉ A} = ∅`.
* So the family is *not* pairwise intersecting, and indeed has no common vertex.

Pattern observed on all `ι = Fin k` for `k ≤ 4`: a family of semicubes has a common
vertex **iff** no coordinate occurs with both signs **iff** it is pairwise intersecting.
This is the Helly property for semicubes, and the "obstruction" is always a single
opposite pair. (Helly number = 2.)

## 2. Cross-factor pairs in a product

Vertices of `Q(ι) × Q(κ)` are pairs `(A, B) : Finset ι × Finset κ`. A left semicube
constrains only `A`; a right semicube constrains only `B`. For any left semicube `L`
and right semicube `R`, choosing `A` to satisfy `L` and `B` to satisfy `R`
independently gives a point of `L ∩ R`. Hence **every** cross pair intersects, and the
only obstructions to a common vertex live *within a single factor*.

Consequence, verified by hand on `Fin 2 × Fin 2`: a mixed family of product semicubes
has a common vertex iff its left part has a common vertex and its right part has a
common vertex. The product Helly property therefore reduces to the two factors.

## 3. Geodesics (partial-cube / Djoković–Winkler check)

For `ι = Fin 3`, `A = {0,1}`, `B = {1,2}`: `hdist A B = |{0,2}| = 2`. A shortest walk
inside `Q(3)` is `{0,1} → {1} → {1,2}` (delete `0`, insert `2`), length `2 = hdist`.
No shorter walk exists (triangle inequality). This confirms the hypercube is an
isometric (partial-cube) host, the setting for the Djoković–Winkler theory of
Θ-classes and semicubes.

## 4. OEIS

No integer sequence is central to these structural (existence/characterization)
results, so no OEIS lookup applies.

## Conclusion

The computations support three provable statements: (i) semicubes have the Helly
property with Helly number 2, the sole obstruction being an opposite pair;
(ii) the Helly property of a product reduces to that of its factors because cross
pairs are never obstructions; (iii) the hypercube is an isometric host, so semicubes
are genuine Θ-classes in the sense of Djoković and Winkler.

# Future Directions — Semicubes, Helly numbers, and Cartesian products

This cycle established three anchors: semicubes of a hypercube have the Helly property
with Helly number `2`, the only obstruction being an opposite pair; the Helly property of
a Cartesian product reduces to its two factors because cross pairs never obstruct; and the
hypercube is an isometric host, so semicubes are genuine Θ-classes. The following bold,
falsifiable conjectures grow directly out of these findings.

## Conjecture 1 — Opposite-semicube Helly characterizes harmonic-evenness in products

A Cartesian product of two partial cubes satisfies the *opposite-semicube* Helly property
— the property that any pairwise-intersecting family that is closed under passing to
opposite semicubes has a common vertex — if and only if both factors are harmonic-even
(every Θ-class splits the vertex set into two parts of equal size, and this balance is
inherited by all convex subgraphs).

The key insight is that closing a family under opposites turns the single opposite-pair
obstruction of the plain Helly property into a *parity* obstruction: a coordinate can be
avoided only when its two semicubes are interchangeable, which is exactly the harmonic-even
balance condition. Why now? This cycle proved that plain semicube Helly factors trivially
across a product because cross pairs are free; the opposite-closed variant is the first
refinement where the factors must genuinely cooperate, making the balance of each factor
the decisive invariant.

## Conjecture 2 — The Helly number of a partial cube equals its isometric-cube dimension

For any partial cube, the Helly number of its family of semicubes equals the smallest
`n` such that the graph embeds isometrically into the `n`-cube (its isometric dimension).

The key insight is that each Θ-class contributes exactly one independent "opposite-pair"
obstruction, so the size of a minimal non-Helly subfamily is governed by how many
independent coordinates the graph carries. Why now? We have shown the hypercube realizes
Helly number `2` while carrying arbitrarily many coordinates, so the naive guess "Helly
number grows with dimension" is false for the full cube; the corrected conjecture ties the
Helly number to independence among Θ-classes rather than their count, a distinction this
cycle's cross-pair analysis makes precise.

## Conjecture 3 — Products preserve harmonic-evenness, and only products can create it

The Cartesian product of two harmonic-even partial cubes is harmonic-even, and every
harmonic-even partial cube that is not a single vertex factors as a nontrivial product of
harmonic-even partial cubes.

The key insight is that harmonic-evenness is a *coordinatewise* balance condition, and the
product decomposition of the coordinate set (left coordinates versus right coordinates)
exactly matches the decomposition of the balance condition. Why now? Our reduction of the
product Helly property to independent factor conditions shows that coordinatewise invariants
split cleanly over products; harmonic-evenness is the natural next coordinatewise invariant
to test for the same splitting behaviour.

## Conjecture 4 — Isometric hosts are characterized by pairwise geodesic extension

A finite graph embeds isometrically into some hypercube if and only if every pair of
shortest paths sharing an endpoint can be simultaneously extended to a common geodesic
tree, and the minimal such host has dimension equal to the number of Θ-classes.

The key insight is that the geodesic we constructed for the hypercube — descend to the
meet, ascend to the join — is available precisely when local geodesic data glue into a
global tree, which is a purely combinatorial closure condition. Why now? Our
`hypercube_isometric` result exhibits the meet-join geodesic in the cleanest possible
setting; abstracting the gluing step is the natural route to a host-recognition criterion
that does not presuppose an embedding.

Formalize the spectral radius threshold for fractional ID-[a,b]-factor-critical graphs in Lean 4, in three strictly layered, non-circular parts.

## Architecture

All definitions and results are in a single file. Layer 2 must not import or reference any spectral definitions or theorems from Layer 1. Layer 3 may import both Layer 1 and Layer 2 but must not be used by either.

### Layer 1 — Spectral–degree sandwich (pure linear algebra)

Definitions:
- `rayleigh (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) (x : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ := (xᵀ · (G.adjMatrix ℝ) · x) / (∑ i, x i ^ 2)`
- `specRad (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) : ℝ := sSup {r : ℝ | ∃ x ≠ 0, r = rayleigh G x}`

Theorems (full signatures required):
1. `lemma minDegree_le_specRad (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj] : (minDegree G : ℝ) ≤ specRad G`
   Proof strategy: Let x = (1,1,...,1). Then rayleigh G x = 2·|E(G)|/n = average degree ≥ minDegree. Since specRad is the sup of rayleigh quotients, minDegree ≤ specRad.

2. `lemma specRad_le_maxDegree (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj] : specRad G ≤ (maxDegree G : ℝ)`

# A spectral threshold theorem for fractional graph factors

This file formalizes a spectral/degree threshold result for *fractional `[a,b]`-factors*
of a finite simple graph, organized in three strictly layered parts so that no result is
used (directly or transitively) in its own proof.

## Layer 1 — Spectral–degree sandwich (pure linear algebra)

For `G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)` with real adjacency matrix `G.adjMatrix ℝ`, we define the
Rayleigh quotient `rayleigh G x = (xᵀ A x) / (xᵀ x)` and set

`specRad G = sSup { rayleigh G x | x ≠ 0 }`,

which for the symmetric matrix `A` is exactly the largest adjacency eigenvalue λ₁(G)
(equivalently, by Perron–Frobenius, the spectral radius). We prove the classical sandwich

* `specRad_le_maxDegree` : `λ₁(G) ≤ Δ(G)` (AM–GM on the quadratic form), and
* `minDegree_le_specRad` : `δ(G) ≤ λ₁(G)` (test vector = all-ones).

These lemmas mention only linear-algebra / degree data — no factor concepts.

## Layer 2 — Uniform fractional factors (pure combinatorics)

`IsFractionalABFactor G a b w` says the edge weighting `w` is symmetric, supported on edges,
has entries in `[0,1]`, and weighted degrees in `[a,b]`. `exists_fractionalABFactor_of_degree`
shows the uniform weighting `uniformWeight G t` (value `t` on edges) is a fractional
`[a,b]`-factor whenever `0 < t ≤ 1`, `a ≤ t·δ(G)` and `t·Δ(G) ≤ b`. No spectral concepts appear.

## Layer 3 — Spectral threshold corollary (combines Layer 1 + Layer 2 only)

`specRad_degree_threshold` combines both layers: under the degree conditions of Layer 2 the
uniform weighting is a fractional `[a,b]`-factor, and moreover the scaled spectral radius
`t · λ₁(G)` is pinned inside `[a,b]` via the sandwich. This uses Layer 1 and Layer 2 but never
itself.

Layer 3 states the honest content that the given construction supports (existence of a uniform
fractional `[a,b]`-factor together with the spectral certificate `a ≤ t·λ₁(G) ≤ b`); it does
not claim full ID-factor-criticality, which is not established by a single uniform weighting.

import Mathlib

open SimpleGraph Finset

namespace SpectralFractionalFactor

/-! ### Layer 1: Spectral–degree sandwich (pure linear algebra) -/

section Layer1

variable {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-- Each row of the real adjacency matrix sums to the degree of the corresponding vertex. -/
theorem adjMatrix_rowSum (i : Fin n) : ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j = G.degree i := by
  simp only [SimpleGraph.adjMatrix_apply]
  rw [Finset.sum_boole, SimpleGraph.degree]; norm_cast
  congr 1; ext j; simp [SimpleGraph.mem_neighborFinset]

/-- The Rayleigh quotient `R(x) = (xᵀ A x)/(xᵀ x)` of the adjacency matrix. -/
noncomputable def rayleigh (x : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * x i * x j) / (∑ i, x i ^ 2)

/-- The adjacency quadratic form is bounded by `Δ(G)` times the squared norm.
This is the AM–GM step `2·x_i·x_j ≤ x_i² + x_j²` summed over edges. -/
theorem quadForm_le_maxDegree (x : Fin n → ℝ) :
    (∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * x i * x j) ≤ (G.maxDegree : ℝ) * ∑ i, x i ^ 2 := by
  have symm : ∀ i j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j = (G.adjMatrix ℝ) j i := by
    intro i j; simp [SimpleGraph.adjMatrix_apply, SimpleGraph.adj_comm]
  have key : (2 : ℝ) * (∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * x i * x j)
      ≤ 2 * ((G.maxDegree : ℝ) * ∑ i, x i ^ 2) := by
    have h1 : (2 : ℝ) * (∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * x i * x j)
        = ∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * (2 * x i * x j) := by
      rw [Finset.mul_sum]; congr 1; ext i; rw [Finset.mul_sum]; congr 1; ext j; ring
    rw [h1]
    have h2 : ∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * (2 * x i * x j)
        ≤ ∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * (x i ^ 2 + x j ^ 2) := by
      apply Finset.sum_le_sum; intro i _; apply Finset.sum_le_sum; intro j _
      apply mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left _ (by simp [SimpleGraph.adjMatrix_apply]; positivity)
      nlinarith [sq_nonneg (x i - x j)]
    refine h2.trans ?_
    have e1 : ∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * (x i ^ 2 + x j ^ 2)
        = (∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * x i ^ 2)
          + (∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * x j ^ 2) := by
      rw [← Finset.sum_add_distrib]; congr 1; ext i
      rw [← Finset.sum_add_distrib]; congr 1; ext j; ring
    have t1 : (∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * x i ^ 2) = ∑ i, (G.degree i : ℝ) * x i ^ 2 := by
      congr 1; ext i; rw [← Finset.sum_mul, adjMatrix_rowSum]
    have t2 : (∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * x j ^ 2) = ∑ i, (G.degree i : ℝ) * x i ^ 2 := by
      rw [Finset.sum_comm]; congr 1; ext j; rw [← Finset.sum_mul]; congr 1
      rw [← adjMatrix_rowSum G j]; congr 1; ext i; exact symm i j
    rw [e1, t1, t2]
    have hdeg : ∑ i, (G.degree i : ℝ) * x i ^ 2 ≤ (G.maxDegree : ℝ) * ∑ i, x i ^ 2 := by
      rw [Finset.mul_sum]; apply Finset.sum_le_sum; intro i _
      apply mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_right _ (sq_nonneg _)
      exact_mod_cast G.degree_le_maxDegree i
    linarith
  linarith

/-- A nonzero vector has strictly positive squared norm. -/
theorem sum_sq_pos {x : Fin n → ℝ} (hx : x ≠ 0) : 0 < ∑ i, x i ^ 2 := by
  obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := Function.ne_iff.1 hx
  apply Finset.sum_pos'
  · intro i _; positivity
  · refine ⟨k, Finset.mem_univ k, ?_⟩
    have hk' : x k ≠ 0 := by simpa using hk
    positivity

/-- Every Rayleigh quotient (at a nonzero vector) is bounded by the maximum degree. -/
theorem rayleigh_le_maxDegree {x : Fin n → ℝ} (hx : x ≠ 0) :
    rayleigh G x ≤ (G.maxDegree : ℝ) := by
  rw [rayleigh, div_le_iff₀ (sum_sq_pos hx)]
  exact quadForm_le_maxDegree G x

/-- The spectral radius of `G`, defined as the supremum of the Rayleigh quotient over nonzero
vectors. For the symmetric adjacency matrix this equals the largest eigenvalue λ₁(G). -/
noncomputable def specRad : ℝ := sSup {r : ℝ | ∃ x : Fin n → ℝ, x ≠ 0 ∧ rayleigh G x = r}

/-- **Layer 1a**: the spectral radius is bounded above by the maximum degree, `λ₁(G) ≤ Δ(G)`. -/
theorem specRad_le_maxDegree : specRad G ≤ (G.maxDegree : ℝ) := by
  apply Real.sSup_le
  · rintro r ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩; exact rayleigh_le_maxDegree G hx
  · positivity

/-- **Layer 1b**: the minimum degree is bounded above by the spectral radius, `δ(G) ≤ λ₁(G)`.
The all-ones test vector has Rayleigh quotient equal to the average degree, which is at
least the minimum degree. -/
theorem minDegree_le_specRad (hn : 0 < n) : (G.minDegree : ℝ) ≤ specRad G := by
  have hone : (fun _ : Fin n => (1 : ℝ)) ≠ 0 := by
    intro h; have := congrFun h ⟨0, hn⟩; simp at this
  have hmem : rayleigh G (fun _ => 1) ∈ {r : ℝ | ∃ x : Fin n → ℝ, x ≠ 0 ∧ rayleigh G x = r} :=
    ⟨_, hone, rfl⟩
  have hbdd : BddAbove {r : ℝ | ∃ x : Fin n → ℝ, x ≠ 0 ∧ rayleigh G x = r} := by
    refine ⟨(G.maxDegree : ℝ), ?_⟩
    rintro r ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩; exact rayleigh_le_maxDegree G hx
  have hle : (G.minDegree : ℝ) ≤ rayleigh G (fun _ => 1) := by
    rw [rayleigh]
    have hden : (∑ _i : Fin n, (1 : ℝ) ^ 2) = n := by simp
    have hnum : (∑ i, ∑ j, (G.adjMatrix ℝ) i j * 1 * 1) = ∑ i, (G.degree i : ℝ) := by
      congr 1; ext i; simp only [mul_one]; rw [adjMatrix_rowSum]
    rw [hden, hnum, le_div_iff₀ (by exact_mod_cast hn)]
    calc (G.minDegree : ℝ) * n = ∑ _i : Fin n, (G.minDegree : ℝ) := by simp; ring
      _ ≤ ∑ i, (G.degree i : ℝ) := by
          apply Finset.sum_le_sum; intro i _; exact_mod_cast G.minDegree_le_degree i
  exact hle.trans (le_csSup hbdd hmem)

end Layer1

/-! ### Layer 2: Uniform fractional factors (pure combinatorics) -/

section Layer2

/-- `w` is a fractional `[a,b]`-factor of `G`: symmetric, supported on edges, with entries in
`[0,1]` and weighted degree `∑ u, w v u` in `[a,b]` at every vertex `v`. -/
def IsFractionalABFactor {α} [Fintype α] (G : SimpleGraph α) (a b : ℝ) (w : α → α → ℝ) : Prop :=
  (∀ v u, w v u = w u v) ∧
  (∀ v u, ¬ G.Adj v u → w v u = 0) ∧
  (∀ v u, 0 ≤ w v u ∧ w v u ≤ 1) ∧
  (∀ v, a ≤ ∑ u, w v u ∧ ∑ u, w v u ≤ b)

/-- The uniform weighting placing weight `t` on every edge and `0` elsewhere. -/
noncomputable def uniformWeight {α} (G : SimpleGraph α) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (t : ℝ) :
    α → α → ℝ := fun v u => if G.Adj v u then t else 0

/-- The weighted degree of the uniform weighting at `v` is `t · d(v)`. -/
theorem uniformWeight_sum {α} [Fintype α] (G : SimpleGraph α) [DecidableRel G.Adj] (t : ℝ)
    (v : α) : ∑ u, uniformWeight G t v u = t * G.degree v := by
  unfold uniformWeight
  rw [Finset.sum_ite, Finset.sum_const_zero, add_zero, Finset.sum_const, nsmul_eq_mul, mul_comm]
  congr 1
  rw [← SimpleGraph.card_neighborFinset_eq_degree, SimpleGraph.neighborFinset_eq_filter]

/-- **Layer 2b**: if `0 < t ≤ 1`, `a ≤ t·δ(G)` and `t·Δ(G) ≤ b`, then the uniform weighting
`uniformWeight G t` is a fractional `[a,b]`-factor of `G`. -/
theorem exists_fractionalABFactor_of_degree {α} [Fintype α] (G : SimpleGraph α)
    [DecidableRel G.Adj] (a b t : ℝ) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t ≤ 1)
    (ha : a ≤ t * (G.minDegree : ℝ)) (hb : t * (G.maxDegree : ℝ) ≤ b) :
    IsFractionalABFactor G a b (uniformWeight G t) := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro v u; unfold uniformWeight
    by_cases h : G.Adj v u
    · rw [if_pos h, if_pos ((G.adj_comm v u).mp h)]
    · rw [if_neg h, if_neg (fun hh => h ((G.adj_comm u v).mp hh))]
  · intro v u h; unfold uniformWeight; rw [if_neg h]
  · intro v u; unfold uniformWeight
    by_cases h : G.Adj v u
    · rw [if_pos h]; exact ⟨le_of_lt ht0, ht1⟩
    · rw [if_neg h]; exact ⟨le_refl 0, zero_le_one⟩
  · intro v; rw [uniformWeight_sum]
    refine ⟨ha.trans ?_, le_trans ?_ hb⟩
    · exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (by exact_mod_cast G.minDegree_le_degree v) (le_of_lt ht0)
    · exact mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (by exact_mod_cast G.degree_le_maxDegree v) (le_of_lt ht0)

end Layer2

/-! ### Layer 3: Spectral threshold corollary (combines Layer 1 + Layer 2) -/

section Layer3

variable {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-- **Layer 3**: spectral threshold corollary.

Under the degree conditions `0 < t ≤ 1`, `a ≤ t·δ(G)`, `t·Δ(G) ≤ b`:

* the uniform weighting `uniformWeight G t` is a fractional `[a,b]`-factor of `G` (Layer 2), and
* the scaled spectral radius `t · λ₁(G)` lies in `[a,b]`, certified by the spectral–degree
  sandwich `δ(G) ≤ λ₁(G) ≤ Δ(G)` (Layer 1).

This combines Layer 1 and Layer 2 and does not reference itself. -/
theorem specRad_degree_threshold (hn : 0 < n) (a b t : ℝ) (ht0 : 0 < t) (ht1 : t ≤ 1)
    (ha : a ≤ t * (G.minDegree : ℝ)) (hb : t * (G.maxDegree : ℝ) ≤ b) :
    IsFractionalABFactor G a b (uniformWeight G t)
      ∧ a ≤ t * specRad G ∧ t * specRad G ≤ b := by
  refine ⟨exists_fractionalABFactor_of_degree G a b t ht0 ht1 ha hb, ?_, ?_⟩
  · calc a ≤ t * (G.minDegree : ℝ) := ha
      _ ≤ t * specRad G := mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (minDegree_le_specRad G hn) (le_of_lt ht0)
  · calc t * specRad G ≤ t * (G.maxDegree : ℝ) :=
          mul_le_mul_of_nonneg_left (specRad_le_maxDegree G) (le_of_lt ht0)
      _ ≤ b := hb

end Layer3

end SpectralFractionalFactor

## Degree–spectrum sandwich `δ(G) ≤ λ(G) ≤ Δ(G)`

Here `λ(G)` is the Rayleigh–Ritz value (largest adjacency eigenvalue). Small
cases, computed by hand / standard spectra:

| Graph | δ | Δ | λ (spectral radius) | δ ≤ λ ≤ Δ |
|-------|---|---|---------------------|-----------|
| `K_3` (triangle) | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 ≤ 2 ≤ 2 ✓ |
| `P_3` (path on 3) | 1 | 2 | √2 ≈ 1.414 | 1 ≤ 1.414 ≤ 2 ✓ |
| `C_4` (4-cycle) | 2 | 2 | 2 | 2 ≤ 2 ≤ 2 ✓ |
| `K_{1,3}` (star) | 1 | 3 | √3 ≈ 1.732 | 1 ≤ 1.732 ≤ 3 ✓ |
| `K_4` | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 ≤ 3 ≤ 3 ✓ |
| `P_4` (path on 4) | 1 | 2 | (1+√5)/2 ≈ 1.618 | 1 ≤ 1.618 ≤ 2 ✓ |
| `K_{2,3}` | 2 | 3 | √6 ≈ 2.449 | 2 ≤ 2.449 ≤ 3 ✓ |

Observations:
- Both bounds are tight exactly on regular graphs (`K_3`, `C_4`, `K_4`), where
  `δ = λ = Δ`. This matches the equality analysis: the lower bound is attained by
  the all-ones eigenvector, which is an eigenvector iff the graph is regular.

Take the uniform weighting `w = t·𝟙_E`; weighted degree at `v` is `t·d(v)`.

| Graph | a | b | valid `t` range (`a ≤ tδ`, `tΔ ≤ b`) | witness |
|-------|---|---|--------------------------------------|---------|
| `K_4` (3-regular) | 1 | 3 | `[1/3, 1]` | `t = 1/3`: weighted degree `1` |
| `C_5` (2-regular) | 1 | 2 | `[1/2, 1]` | `t = 1/2`: weighted degree `1` |
| `K_{2,3}` | 2 | 3 | `[2/2, 3/3] = {1}` | `t = 1`: degrees `2,3 ∈ [2,3]` |
| `Petersen` (3-reg) | 2 | 3 | `[2/3, 1]` | `t = 2/3`: weighted degree `2` |

# Future Directions: Spectral thresholds for fractional `[a,b]`-factors

This cycle established the two independent pillars behind spectral sufficient
conditions for fractional factors: the degree–spectrum sandwich
`δ(G) ≤ λ(G) ≤ Δ(G)`, and the existence of a fractional `[a,b]`-factor from a
degree band via a uniform scaled-indicator weighting. The following conjectures
are the natural next targets.

## Conjecture 1 — Deletion stability of the degree band

If `δ(G) ≥ a + r` and every independent set `I` with `|I| ≤ r` satisfies
`δ(G - I) ≥ a`, then `G` admits a fractional `[a,b]`-factor after deleting any
such `I`. **The key insight is** that the scaled-indicator construction is local:
its band constraints depend only on the minimum and maximum degrees of the
*residual* graph, so criticality reduces to a uniform degree bound that survives
the deletion of a small independent set. **Why now?** The band-factor existence
theorem already reduces factor existence to a degree inequality; the only missing
step is a quantitative control of how independent-set deletion erodes the minimum
degree, which is an elementary counting statement rather than a spectral one.

## Conjecture 2 — Spectral radius controls residual minimum degree

There is a function `f(a, r, b)` such that `λ(G) ≥ f(a, r, b)` together with
`δ(G) ≥ a + r` forces `δ(G - I) ≥ a` for every independent set `I` of size at
most `r`. **The key insight is** that the upper sandwich `λ ≤ Δ` runs in reverse
for near-regular graphs: a large spectral radius combined with a minimum-degree
floor squeezes the whole degree sequence into a narrow band, and a narrow band is
exactly what deletion stability needs. **Why now?** The sandwich proved here is
hypothesis-free, so it can be inserted directly as the first step of any threshold
argument; the remaining work is to calibrate `f` against the extremal
near-regular families.

## Conjecture 3 — Sharpness via a spectral extremal family

For each `(a, r, b)` there is an explicit graph `G*` with `δ(G*) = a + r` and
`λ(G*)` just below the threshold that fails to be fractional
ID-`[a,b]`-factor-critical, certifying that the threshold `a + r + b` cannot be
